title: Business Loans in Ontario: Options, Rates, and How to Qualify
excerpt: Ontario businesses can borrow from about $5K to $1.15M. Compare bank, CSBFP, BDC, and alternative lenders by rate, amount, and speed — and see how to qualify.
content:
Ontario businesses can borrow anywhere from about $5,000 to $1.15 million, depending on the lender and program. Banks and credit unions offer the lowest rates; federal programs like the CSBFP and BDC sit in the middle; and private/alternative lenders fund fastest (often in 1–5 business days) at a higher cost.

Whether you run a logistics company in Mississauga, a restaurant in Toronto, a manufacturer in Hamilton, or a tech startup in the Waterloo region, your financing options are broadly the same across Ontario — but the right one depends on how fast you need the money, how much you qualify for, and what the loan is for. Here is a plain-English guide to your options, realistic rates and amounts, and how to qualify.

What business loan options are available in Ontario?

Ontario businesses can choose from four main avenues: bank and credit-union loans, federally backed programs, private/alternative lenders, and provincial/regional small-business support. Most of these programs are delivered the same way across the country, so Ontario companies have full access to the national lending market.

1. Banks and credit unions

The major banks and Ontario credit unions offer term loans, operating lines of credit, and commercial mortgages at the lowest rates. They also have the strictest requirements — typically two or more years in business, strong credit, and full financial statements — so approval is slower and harder for newer firms.

2. Federal programs (available in Ontario)

Two national programs are widely used by Ontario businesses. The Canada Small Business Financing Program (CSBFP) is delivered by regular banks and credit unions but partly guaranteed by the federal government (reported at up to 85% of a lender's loss), which makes lenders more willing to say yes. Per Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, the maximum is roughly $1.15 million per borrower (term loans up to about $1 million, lines of credit up to about $150,000), with floating rates capped around prime plus 3%. Confirm current caps and rate limits with ISED or your lender before applying.

The Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) is a federal Crown corporation that lends directly. Its online Small Business Loan goes up to about $350,000, priced as a floating base rate plus a risk margin set for your business (BDC does not publish a fixed rate), with no prepayment penalties. Larger BDC financing is available case by case.

3. Private and alternative lenders

Alternative lenders — including online lenders and marketplaces — are the fastest and most flexible option, and the easiest to qualify for, but they cost more. Typical amounts range from about $5,000 to $500,000 (some marketplaces arrange up to $800,000), with funding often in 1–5 business days. This is the category most Ontario owners turn to when a bank says no or moves too slowly. True North matches businesses with offers from $5K to $800K across this market.

4. Provincial and regional small-business support

Ontario does not run a single province-wide business loan the way the federal programs work, but it offers meaningful support. The province's network of Small Business Enterprise Centres (SBECs) — around 47 locations across Ontario — delivers advice, training, and the Starter Company Plus program (mentorship, training, and a grant of up to about $5,000 for eligible new or expanding businesses). In rural and northern Ontario, Community Futures Development Corporations (funded federally through FedDev Ontario in the south and FedNor in the north) can provide loans reported at up to about $150,000. Eligibility and amounts are decided locally, so confirm current details with your nearest centre.

How much can an Ontario business borrow?

It depends on the product and your financials. Alternative lenders generally start around $5,000; federal programs and banks can reach into seven figures for established, well-qualified businesses. The table below shows typical ranges by loan type.

What interest rates do Ontario business loans carry?

Rates depend far more on the lender and your profile than on the fact that you are in Ontario. As a rough guide: banks and the CSBFP are cheapest (CSBFP floating rates are capped around prime plus 3%), BDC prices on a floating base rate plus a risk margin, and private/alternative lenders are the most expensive — sometimes substantially so.

Alternative products are often quoted as a factor rate or fee rather than an annual percentage rate, which can hide the true cost. Always convert any quote to an effective annual rate before comparing, and read the fee schedule. Because pricing moves with the Bank of Canada's policy rate and with lender appetite, treat any published number as indicative and confirm current terms with the lender.

What do Ontario lenders require to qualify?

Most lenders look at the same core factors, with banks demanding the most and alternative lenders the least. In general, be ready to show:

  • Time in business — banks usually want 2+ years; many alternative lenders accept 6–12 months.
  • Revenue — monthly or annual sales, often with a minimum threshold (e.g., several thousand dollars a month for alternative lenders).
  • Bank statements — typically the last 3–6 months to confirm cash flow.
  • Credit — personal and/or business credit; stronger credit unlocks lower rates.
  • Business registration — a registered Ontario business (sole proprietorship, partnership, or corporation) and, often, a business bank account.
  • Purpose and plan — especially for banks, the CSBFP, and BDC, a clear use of funds and a reasonable plan.

Farming businesses are excluded from the CSBFP, and some lenders avoid specific industries, so check fit before you apply.

How fast can you get funded in Ontario?

Speed varies widely by lender. Alternative and online lenders can approve and fund in as little as 1–5 business days; BDC's smaller loans are often decided within a couple of weeks; and traditional bank or CSBFP loans can take several weeks because of their deeper underwriting. To move faster, have your bank statements and business details ready and apply through a single matched lender rather than shopping many at once. See how our matching process works.

Which loan is right for your Ontario business?

A simple way to decide: match the product to the need. For general working capital or a short-term opportunity, a small business term loan is the workhorse. To buy vehicles or machinery, equipment financing spreads the cost over the asset's life and often uses the equipment as collateral. If you have strong daily card or online sales but thin credit, a merchant cash advance trades a higher cost for speed and flexible repayment. For the lowest rates and you can wait, start with your bank or a CSBFP application.

Where in Ontario can you get a business loan?

Everywhere. Because the federal programs and national alternative lenders operate across the province, a business in Toronto, Ottawa, Mississauga, Hamilton, London, Kitchener–Waterloo, Windsor, or a smaller northern community has access to the same core products. Local SBECs and Community Futures offices add in-person advice and, in some regions, dedicated loans — useful if you are just starting out or based in a rural or northern area.

Frequently asked questions

Can a new business get a loan in Ontario?

Yes, though options are narrower. Banks usually want two or more years of history, but many alternative lenders fund businesses with 6–12 months of revenue, and startups can look at BDC, the CSBFP, and local Starter Company Plus support delivered through Ontario's Small Business Enterprise Centres.

Are there government-backed business loans in Ontario?

Yes. The Canada Small Business Financing Program (CSBFP) is partly guaranteed by the federal government and delivered through ordinary banks and credit unions, and the BDC is a federal Crown corporation that lends directly. Both are fully available to Ontario businesses. Confirm current caps and rates with the program before applying.

What credit score do I need for a business loan in Ontario?

There is no single cutoff. Banks and government-backed programs generally expect good personal and business credit, while many alternative lenders weigh recent revenue and cash flow more heavily and can work with weaker credit — usually at a higher rate.

How much does a business loan cost in Ontario?

It ranges from near prime (bank and CSBFP loans) to considerably higher for fast alternative products. Because many alternative lenders quote a factor rate or flat fee, convert every offer to an effective annual rate and compare total repayment, not just the headline number.

Do I need collateral for an Ontario business loan?

Not always. Equipment financing and commercial mortgages are secured by the asset, and larger bank loans often require security, but many alternative term loans and merchant cash advances are unsecured — relying on revenue and a personal guarantee instead.
